articles.title: Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers
articles.summary: The post Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers appeared first on ProPublica.
articles.body:
When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world's largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump's tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers.

The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports.

Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients:

The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.

Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist.

Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses.

The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they've asked for, and it has denied ProPublica's requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.

Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, "returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing," though they generally don't say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups.

But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers.

"Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn't anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund," said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. "It really explains why it's so important for the government, when they're doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don't pay extra money and not get it back."

articles.title: Microsoft staff wrote open letter that they fear being replaced by AI, then 60,000 got exit offers; Satya Nadella now says: Why do we need software engineers? To...
articles.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has given his clearest explanation yet for why the company asked around 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its
articles.body: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has given his clearest explanation yet for why the company asked around 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its workforce, to consider leaving. Speaking to Andrew Ross Sorkin at the NYT DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Nadella said the buyout was meant “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices” as Microsoft rebuilds itself around AI. His comments come weeks after a group of Microsoft workers circulated an open letter. It accused the company of chasing AI with a “speed-at-all-costs” ethos and flagged “threats of AI job replacement and layoffs.”Nadella made it clear that the plan is not to swap engineers for AI.“Let’s take software engineering. We went from, ‘Well, we don’t buy that AI can ever do software.’ To suddenly, ‘Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?’ To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point,” he said.Some people, he admitted, find “that reorganization and change is sort of hard,” but “it has to be done.”Nadella says every job at Microsoft will turn into managing AI agentsTo show what that new operating point looks like, Nadella pointed to the team behind Cowork, the AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps. The team has just 11 developers, and they have learnt to let AI do most of the building. “They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product,” he said.He expects every employee to eventually direct AI agents instead of doing the work themselves. “That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs,” Nadella said. He also admitted that a 51-year-old company was not born AI-first, and that the shift “is going to take a bit more time than anyone expects.”On a podcast with Gergely Orosz last week, he went a step further. He said the industry had “created enormous anxiety” among workers with talk of the singularity and of AI taking away all jobs.Microsoft employees had already put their AI worries in writingBefore the buyouts were announced, current and former employees circulated a letter signed “Concerned Microsoft Workers.” It called working at the company “joyless and demoralizing.” According to the letter, staff were pushed to use AI in almost every area with little training, and were spending time “fixing AI slop” and reworking low-quality features.The letter asked Microsoft to involve workers in decisions on AI and to stop tying AI use to rewards, reprimands or layoffs. It also asked the company to treat AI as an assistive tool rather than “a complete labor replacement.”Six employees told the NYT that the buyout landed on a workforce already strained by AI targets and stagnant pay, with some merit raises this year below 1%. Gretchen Thomas, a design leader who left in September, had her stock award cut. According to a memo seen by the NYT, part of the reason was that she did “not consistently” show speed, urgency and willingness to experiment, including with AI.Microsoft’s 60,000 buyout offer covers teams in India, US, Canada and UKMicrosoft confirmed the Voluntary Exit Offer on October 26. It covers employees at vice president level and below on select teams in the US, Canada, India and the UK. Xbox, Windows, Copilot and Finance are among the divisions involved.Employees have until December 9 to decide, and those who accept will leave on December 31 with at least eight weeks of base pay. Microsoft expects fewer than 5% to take it. This is its second buyout this year, after a retirement-age offer earlier in 2026. It also follows layoffs of 10,000 people in 2023, over 15,000 in 2025 and about 4,800 this summer.Chief people officer Amy Coleman told the NYT that the buyouts were not linked to how AI is changing work, and she did not rule out future layoffs. Two days after the offer, Microsoft reported quarterly profit of $36.6 billion, up 32%. Capital spending, mostly on data centres, rose 30% to $45.2 billion, and the company expects to spend roughly $170 billion this year.For those who stay, the worry is more immediate. Employees told the NYT they do not expect departing colleagues to be replaced, so their work will land on the people left behind. That is where Nadella’s new operating point will be tested first.Fearless legend or grounded realist? Rate yourself on 11 categories in the Great Indian Confidence Survey – find out in 3–6 min

articles.title: Hackers use Microsoft Outlook security flaw to steal your login data
articles.summary: Microsoft Outlook flaw CVE-2026-124194 lets a malicious .msg file expose NTLMv2 authentication data, and Microsoft confirms hackers already exploited it.
articles.body: You probably know better than to enter your password on a suspicious website. But what if hackers could steal information tied to your Windows login without ever asking for your password? That's the concern behind a Microsoft Outlook security flaw that hackers are already exploiting. Attackers can trick someone into opening a malicious Outlook file that quietly exposes Windows authentication information. That information could help a criminal impersonate you and potentially gain access to systems you use. Microsoft released a fix on Nov. 10. However, the company confirms hackers were exploiting the vulnerability before the update became available. If you use Outlook for work, this is one security update you should check right away. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. FAKE AI EVENT INVITES TARGET MICROSOFT AND GOOGLE LOGINS How hackers exploit the Microsoft Outlook security flaw The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, involves how Outlook handles specially crafted message files. An attacker can create a malicious Outlook message file, such as one using the .msg format. The hacker then needs to convince someone to open that file in an affected version of Outlook. Once opened, the malicious file can cause Outlook to connect to a server controlled by the attacker. That connection happens without the usual warning about accessing external content. During the connection, Windows can reveal NTLMv2 authentication information. This data helps Windows verify your identity when connecting to certain network services. The information differs from your actual password. However, hackers may be able to use it in a follow-up attack to impersonate you. For someone using Outlook at work, that could potentially expose company resources their account can access. The outcome depends on the network's security protections and whether the attacker can successfully misuse the authentication information. Here's what makes this especially concerning. The attack doesn't require you to type your password into a fake login page. Opening the malicious file can be enough if your computer can connect to the attacker's network location. Microsoft says simply viewing the message through Outlook's Preview Pane does not trigger this particular vulnerability. Someone must open the malicious file for the attack to work. Microsoft confirms hackers are already exploiting the flaw Microsoft included the Outlook fix in its November Patch Tuesday security updates. The company's core release addressed 1,093 vulnerabilities, including 63 rated critical. Interestingly, Microsoft classified this particular Outlook vulnerability as moderate, giving it a CVSS severity score of 6.5 out of 10. However, that rating tells only part of the story. Microsoft confirms attackers have already exploited the flaw. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) also added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov. 10. In other words, hackers are already taking advantage of this security weakness. Microsoft has not publicly identified who carried out the attacks or disclosed how many people were affected. The company also hasn't provided detailed information about the incidents. With hackers already exploiting the flaw, it's important to install the security update as soon as possible. FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN Who is affected by the Outlook security vulnerability? According to Microsoft's security advisory, the affected products include: The vulnerability concerns affected desktop Office installations on Windows computers. Microsoft's advisory does not list Outlook.com in a web browser or the Outlook mobile apps as affected products. If your employer manages your Microsoft 365 software, your IT department may handle these updates. However, it's worth confirming that the security fix has been installed. For people who manage their own computers, here's how to check. How to protect yourself from the Outlook security flaw The most important thing you can do is update Microsoft Office. However, a few additional precautions can help reduce your exposure to suspicious files and account attacks. 1) Update Microsoft Office immediately Microsoft has released security updates addressing the vulnerability. You can manually check for updates in supported Windows versions of Office. If you don't see Update Now, you may need to select Enable Updates first. If the entire Update Options menu is missing, your employer may manage updates centrally. Contact your IT department rather than assuming the software has already been patched. You can also review Microsoft's official Office update instructions. 2) Confirm your Microsoft Office version After installing the update, you can check which version of Office is running on your computer. For affected volume-licensed installations, Microsoft's November 10 security release includes these updated builds: These build numbers apply to the specified LTSC editions. They shouldn't be used to check other Office versions. If you're using Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, the correct build depends on your organization's update channel. You can check Microsoft's Office security release notes or contact your IT department to confirm the fix. 3) Check for Windows security updates Although this vulnerability requires an Office fix, keeping Windows updated remains important. On Windows 11: Next, check whether Windows can receive updates for other Microsoft products. This can help Windows deliver updates for supported Microsoft products. However, some Office installations receive updates through separate services or employer-managed systems. Remember that checking Windows Update alone may not confirm you've installed the specific Outlook fix. Check Office separately. It's also smart to back up important files before installing major operating system updates. 4) Be suspicious of unexpected Outlook attachments A message file from an unfamiliar sender deserves extra caution, especially if you weren't expecting it. Watch for attachments ending in .msg, a common file format for saved Outlook messages. The format itself is legitimate. However, attackers can abuse it to deliver this exploit. If an email claims you need to open an attached message to review an invoice or urgent workplace request, verify it through another trusted channel. Even attachments appearing to come from coworkers deserve a second look when the request seems unusual. 5) Report suspicious emails in Outlook If something looks suspicious, avoid opening the attachment. Instead, report the message using Outlook's built-in reporting tools when available. In supported versions of Outlook: The exact menu location depends on your Outlook version and your employer's settings. If you're using a work account and don't see a reporting option, contact your IT department. Avoid forwarding the suspicious attachment to other coworkers. 6) Use strong antivirus protection Strong antivirus software can help identify suspicious attachments and malicious activity before they cause further damage. Look for protection that includes real-time scanning and behavior-based detection. These features may help catch threats that traditional virus signatures miss. However, antivirus software cannot replace Microsoft's security patch. Installing the Outlook update remains essential for closing this particular vulnerability. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 7) Turn on multifactor authentication Multifactor authentication (MFA) adds another layer of account protection by requiring additional verification when you sign in. Enable it on your Microsoft account and other important services whenever available. Keep in mind that MFA may not stop attacks involving stolen Windows authentication information. That's another reason updating Outlook takes priority. Know what to do if you opened a suspicious file If you recently opened an unexpected Outlook message attachment, don't assume everything is fine because nothing unusual appeared on your screen. Here's what to do next. One important reminder: Changing your password alone may not address every potential exposure from this vulnerability. If you opened the attachment on a work computer, let your IT team determine whether additional security measures are necessary. Why Microsoft's latest security update deserves attention Microsoft's November security release covers far more than Outlook. It also fixes weaknesses that could allow attackers to gain additional privileges or remotely execute malicious code. For those of you using a Windows PC every day, the sheer number of vulnerabilities may sound overwhelming. However, not every flaw carries the same immediate risk. In this case, the Outlook weakness deserves your attention because Microsoft has confirmed active exploitation. The larger concern is how easily a malicious file can take advantage of trusted software. Outlook is part of everyday communication for countless businesses, and opening saved email messages may seem harmless. This vulnerability shows why keeping Office updated deserves the same attention as updating Windows. Kurt's key takeaways What concerns me about this Outlook flaw is how little someone has to do to put their information at risk. You could receive what looks like a routine work attachment, open it and unknowingly expose information that helps a hacker impersonate you. There's no obvious warning telling you something went wrong. And by the time you realize it, the damage may already be done. I also find it troubling that Microsoft rated this vulnerability moderate even though attackers were already exploiting it. Most people aren't going to spend their day reviewing security ratings, and they shouldn't have to. They need software that protects them and updates that are easy to install. My advice is simple. If you use Outlook on a Windows computer, check for Office updates today. Don't assume your computer has already taken care of it. Should Microsoft be doing more to prevent a single malicious Outlook file from exposing your login information, or do you think keeping your software updated is enough protection? articles.title: UN court cites military Facebook posts while finding Myanmar guilty of genocide
articles.summary: In its ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya Muslim population in 2016 and 2017, the United Nations says Facebook played a role in spreading hate speech.
articles.body: In its ruling that Myanmar committed state-sponsored genocide against the Rohingya people in 2016 and 2017, the United Nations’ top court says that Facebook played a role in helping Myanmar’s military spread hate speech against its Muslim minority. The ruling from the International Court of Justice determined that Facebook posts made by the country’s military “dehumanized” the Muslim minority “and at times encouraged and legitimized violence against them,” as reported earlier by Reuters. The decision that Myanmar committed genocide comes after The Gambia sued the country in 2019 over the military’s violent “clearance operations” targeting the Rohingya Muslims. The military relied heavily on Facebook, which was the most popular platform in Myanmar at the time of the attacks, with a 2022 report from Amnesty International finding that the platform “proactively amplified and promoted content on the Facebook platform which incited violence, hatred, and discrimination against the Rohingya.” Despite numerous warnings from human rights activists, Amnesty International said Facebook failed to stop the spread of hateful content in Myanmar. The UN is now backing up these findings. It cites a report from the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), which says that a post made by the military ahead of its August 25th, 2017 massacres on the Rohingya people “unleashed a torrent of public vitriol,” with over 200 comments calling for Rohingya people “to be shot, killed, exterminated or permanently removed from Myanmar.” Facebook later removed military-linked pages containing thousands of posts with anti-Rohingya hate speech published between July and December 2017, according to the IIMM. The company admitted in 2018 that it didn’t do enough to prevent the incitement of violence in Myanmar, and later introduced a “corporate human rights policy” that includes an annual report about its impact on human rights. The Verge reached out to Meta with a request for comment but didn’t immediately hear back.

articles.title: Justice Department clears NextEra-Dominion merger
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Thursday greenlighted the merger between energy companies NextEra and Dominion, after noting concerns about the deal’s potential impact on electricity costs. The DOJ said in a release the Internal Market Monitor of ISO New England — an entity that oversees the region’s electric power system — submitted comments to…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Thursday greenlighted the merger between energy companies NextEra and Dominion, after noting concerns about the deal’s potential impact on electricity costs .

The DOJ said in a release the Internal Market Monitor of ISO New England — an entity that oversees the region’s electric power system — submitted comments to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), which is tasked with approving the NextEra-Dominion merger.

Those comments, the DOJ noted, warned the deal “might give the merged firm the incentive and ability to deactivate” an electricity plant that is “still economically viable.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The combined entity would do so to “increase capacity payments” in the New England region, the Internal Market Monitor claimed.

Dominion and NextEra announced the nearly $67 billion merger in May, in a deal the two companies said would create the world’s largest regulated electric utility business by market capitalization. The companies said in May they anticipated closing in 12 to 18 months.

To alleviate the Internal Market Monitor’s concerns to FERC, the companies granted the regulator the authority to investigate “any plant that the merged firm proposes to deactivate” for five years starting in May 2028, the DOJ stated.

Under the agreement, the Internal Market Monitor could bar Florida-based NextEra from deactivating a plant it determines to still have “economic value.”

Given that, the DOJ’s Antitrust Division closed its probe into the merger. The Federal Trade Commission can also raise antitrust concerns about mergers.

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) in October called for the combined NextEra-Dominion entity to halt electricity rate hikes for six years if the deal goes through. Dominion is headquartered in Richmond, Va.

The Virginia State Corporation Commission must also approve the merger before the two sides can complete it. Opening arguments in the state regulator’s legal review of the deal took place on Tuesday.

Rising utility bills posed a political issue for the GOP this midterm cycle , as Democrats swept to clinch control of Congress and nabbed a majority of governor’s mansions for the first time in 16 years.

Electricity prices increased by 0.9 percent from September to October, the highest monthly increase since April, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported.

articles.title: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Exclusive: A simple security lapse exposed transcriptions of police interviews and bodycam footage on a cloud server without a password.
articles.body:
A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.

The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.

According to Anurag Sen , a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.

The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.

Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.

Sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”

From his island home in Indonesia, Sen has uncovered sensitive U.S. military emails spilling from a compartmentalized Department of Defense cloud server; databases exposing reams of customer records ; the inner workings of a country’s national license plate surveillance system ; and public systems that inadvertently sent out streams of SMS codes used by people around the world to log into their online accounts.

Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.

Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.

“We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, said in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”

“We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.

The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.

It’s unclear if the company has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.

Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.

The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes.

Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors.

“An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted.

Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the new wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web.

Similar to Amazon’s recent efforts to make it difficult to make S3 buckets public without going through clear multistep warnings, newer vibe-coding platforms like Lovable and Supabase have also made changes to their platforms to prevent user mistakes.

“Everyone often fears shadowy hackers,” Sen said. But he argues that the real crisis is leaving sensitive systems and databases “wide open to the public internet without a password.”

articles.title: 'Generational theft': Harsh pushback follows a plan to fund Social Security with more government borrowing
articles.summary: A plan to pay Social Security benefits with even more government borrowing has drawn harsh pushback from budget experts.
articles.body:
A new plan to pay Social Security benefits with even more government borrowing has drawn harsh pushback from budget experts, who note it would make America's debt exponentially worse and fail to fix the underlying problem.

Republican Sen. Ron Johnson introduced a bill this week that would forestall any cuts in benefits by authorizing transfers from the US Treasury in the event of a shortfall in Social Security's main Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OADSI) Trust Fund.

The bill has little chance of passage, but this week's contretemps illustrates Washington's current lack of readiness to confront the Social Security shortfall that is projected to be felt during the next presidential term.

An array of budget experts dismissed Johnson's plan as unserious. They say solutions are urgently needed before the program is depleted in about six years — but that this isn't it.

"Let's be clear: Senator Johnson's proposal would add $45 trillion (!) to the national debt through three decades," wrote Jessica Riedl, a budget and tax fellow at the Brookings Institution, calling it "generational theft."

"This isn't Social Security reform. It isn't even a nothingburger. It is actually anti-reform," said Douglas Holtz-Eakin, a former director of the Congressional Budget Office, calling it "a terrible step in the wrong direction."

Johnson, for his part, was unapologetic, writing on X , "My Stop Scaring Seniors Act simply prevents Social Security benefits from being reduced when the trust fund is depleted."

But with the US already more than $40 trillion in debt , Johnson's bill would need to be funded by more government borrowing which — the bill specifies — would not count toward US debt ceiling calculations.

"Not only does the legislation automate congressional malfeasance, it evades any congressionally set limits on that malfeasance," Holtz-Eakin added.

The Social Security program's trustees currently estimate that the program will face a shortfall by 2032, which, under current law, would force benefits to be cut by roughly 22% .

Experts for years have urged lawmakers to avert this shortfall through some combination of increasing revenue and the hot-button topic of reducing benefits.

Social Security is funded through payroll taxes. One fix often pushed by Democrats is to raise the taxable income cap, which rises to $192,300 in 2027 . Earnings above that amount are not subject to the tax, a break for wealthier Americans.

articles.body:
Reps. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif.) and Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), ranking member on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, are pressing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for information about the agency’s investigation into Megaspeed.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company, is facing a probe from the Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice (DOJ) over whether it helped smuggle advanced AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.

But Commerce’s role in the investigation has come under scrutiny after The New York Times reported that Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, reached out to agents working on the case last year.

Teter reportedly said Under Secretary of Commerce Jeff Kessler had given the company permission to reach out. Kessler heads the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which oversees export controls.

“The American public and Congress deserve a full accounting of what happened,” Kamlager-Dove and Meeks wrote in a letter to Lutnick on Thursday.

The case was transferred to the DOJ shortly after Teter’s outreach, according to the Times. The agencies said in a joint statement Monday that the Justice Department “took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed” following an on-site inspection of the company last June.

The lawmakers called for answers as to “whether Under Secretary Kessler permitted or encouraged Nvidia to contact BIS agents actively investigating transactions in which the company was involved, and whether the Department allowed a major American corporation that is financially and personally linked to the Trump Administration to interfere with law enforcement activity.”

They are seeking information about when the BIS launched its investigation into Megaspeed, what information was gathered, whether the probe was halted, what communications Kessler had with Nvidia about Megaspeed and whether Nvidia received any nonpublic information.

“The Department of Commerce has a responsibility to protect American national security, enforce export control laws, and ensure that no corporation receives preferential treatment in matters involving potential violations of federal law,” they added.

The Senate voted late Thursday night to pass a law that seeks to speed up the nation’s energy and infrastructure build-out, including by loosening its environmental laws.

The bill was a bipartisan push, spearheaded by Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) and Mike Lee (R-Utah).

Nevertheless, most Democrats opposed the law, citing among their concerns its loosening of environmental laws, lessening of tribal input into projects that may impact them and potential to bolster fossil fuel production and infrastructure.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The bill makes changes to the Clean Water Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act.

This includes language that makes it harder for the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and states to block projects on environmental grounds.

It also includes language exempting certain activities, including expansions to natural gas pipelines; makes it more difficult for opponents of a project to sue over it; extends how long water quality permits can last before they need to be renewed; and adds hurdles to the EPA’s ability to set water quality criteria.

It also changes the Endangered Species Act, including a change to the definition of “best available science,” which is required to be used to determine whether a species should get legal protections, in a way that environmentalists say creates a high threshold for protections.

These fourteen Democrats voted for it: Whitehouse, Heinrich and Sens. Chris Coons (Del.), John Fetterman (Pa.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), John Hickenlooper (Colo.), Amy Klobuchar (Minn.), Gary Peters (Mich.), Jack Reed (R.I.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Chuck Schumer (N.Y.), Elissa Slotkin (Mich.) and Mark Warner (Va.). Also among the yes votes was Sen. Angus King (I-Maine), who caucuses with Democrats.

The bill also contains significant wins for Democrats on climate and renewable energy — and the bill’s Democratic supporters point to analyses showing that it’s actually projected to bring down U.S. emissions.

Among the key provisions expected to bolster solar and wind power is a new authority granted to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission allowing it to approve new power lines when states choose not to, which is expected to help get more renewable power onto the grid.

It also contains provisions that would force data centers to pay for any electricity cost increases their demand would cause. Supporters of the bill have pointed to one analysis saying it will save consumers $50 to $78 per year on their electric bills in 2040.

Whitehouse and Heinrich have been championing the legislation, calling it a win for the climate as well as affordability.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will get more affordable energy onto the grid faster, make data centers pay their fair share of electricity and grid costs, and create more than 100,000 good-paying American jobs — all while maintaining important environmental protections and strengthening Tribal consultation,” Heinrich said in a statement on the legislation.

“This bill kicks off Democrats bringing down energy costs, lowering emissions, creating well-paying jobs, and ending the free ride for data centers,” Whitehouse said in his own statement. “Americans will quickly begin getting some relief on their energy bills if the House follows suit.”

Other Democratic and Democratic-caucusing supporters seemed torn. In a statement shared with The Hill, King said his vote “wasn’t an easy choice.”

“I listened to my environmental friends in Maine, many of whom were opposed to the bill. I talked to people in the energy field, particularly in the renewable field, and decided that on balance this bill is a lot better than the status quo,” King said.

“This bill unlocks an enormous amount of renewable energy that is now basically unable to get to the market because of a lack of transmission,” he added.

articles.title: Bessent says Jensen Huang did not come up during China discussions
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not a topic of discussion between U.S. and Chinese officials during a summit in China this week. When CNBC’s Sara Eisen asked the Treasury secretary whether the tech mogul came up in conversations, he replied, “No.” President Trump met with Chinese President…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not a topic of discussion between U.S. and Chinese officials during a summit in China this week.

When CNBC’s Sara Eisen asked the Treasury secretary whether the tech mogul came up in conversations, he replied , “No.”

President Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week , days after Huang departed Nvidia amid reports about his extramarital affairs — including one with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

Jensen Huang had successfully lobbied the Trump administration to ease export controls on Nvidia’s chips, allowing the company to sell them to China.

Bessent said Friday that Nvidia’s H200 chips are the “threshold level” of chips the firm can sell to China.

“That continues as planned and … everything beneath there,” the Treasury secretary added on “Squawk Box.”

In the wake of Huang’s resignation , Nvidia’s board of directors formed a committee to oversee export controls. The committee will receive legal, national security and trade compliance advice from outside experts, the company noted in a Tuesday release .

Bessent, however, said he does not “anticipate” a change in the administration’s policy regarding export controls on Nvidia’s chips.

“President Trump was very clear when he made the policy. He drew a very firm line at the H200s, and believes that is the level that China should be able to get.”

Trump, who has backed Huang’s return to Nvidia , told Fox News on Wednesday he “ might have ” brought up the situation “briefly” with Xi.

“It’s such a tragedy,” he told Jacqui Heinrich, calling Huang a “brilliant man.”

articles.title: Environmental groups sue to block Army’s lead detonation at Iowa ammunition plant
articles.summary: Two environmental groups are suing the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in a bid to stop the Army from detonating thousands of pounds of explosive lead material at an Iowa ammunition plant, arguing the activity could expose thousands of families in the surrounding communities to toxic dust. The Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter are challenging an emergency…
articles.body:
Two environmental groups are suing the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in a bid to stop the Army from detonating thousands of pounds of explosive lead material at an Iowa ammunition plant, arguing the activity could expose thousands of families in the surrounding communities to toxic dust.

The Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter are challenging an emergency permit issued by the EPA that authorized the detonation of 68 drums of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.

“The Army left 68 drums of a primary explosive to degrade for roughly two decades until it decided that the only safe option became detonating them near populated areas,” the complaint states. “That turned the Army’s storage management failure into a public health event for people in at least two states.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Lawyers argue the EPA unlawfully bypassed environmental regulations in approving the permit, including that less dangerous alternatives were not fully considered, and it failed to require conditions “necessary to protect human health and the environment.”

They also claim the public was not given an opportunity to weigh in, noting that notice of the plan came less than a week before the scheduled detonations.

“It very well could be the case that the U.S. Army has no other safe alternative to disposing of the toxic lead azide,” Sarah Green, executive director for the Iowa Environmental Council, said in a statement. “But our federal government needs to do better at communicating the potential health risks of lead contamination in our communities and providing more time to keep our communities and vulnerable groups safe, like children and pregnant women.”

The groups asked the court to halt the explosions, which were originally scheduled for Friday, while its challenge to the permit plays out.

The acting Army secretary announced on Thursday that the controlled explosions would be postponed until Monday after lawmakers and residents complained about the short notice .

“This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material,” acting Army Secretary Adam Telle wrote in a post on the social platform X.

The EPA, Army and Department of Health and Human Services wrote in a joint update on Friday that they are working to ensure the explosions are “conducted in the safest fashion possible.”

“Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” the agency wrote.

The lawsuit states that the detonations would release elevated levels of lead dust into the air that could extend 100 miles north of the ammunition plant, leaving it to linger in “yards, gardens, and play areas” for years to come.

Inhaling or swallowing lead is highly dangerous to animals and humans, particularly children, and can pose serious health risks, according to the EPA. There are no known safe levels of exposure.

“Lead dust in the air will not just disappear once it settles to the ground — people, cattle, chickens and wildlife will continue to face exposures to lead from soil, water runoff, and deposition into waterbodies,” the complaint states.

articles.title: Lisa Cook warns the Fed could get behind the curve if it doesn't raise rates now
articles.summary: Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook said Friday that the central bank risks getting behind the curve in bringing inflation down if it doesn't raise interest r...
articles.body:
Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook said Friday that the central bank risks getting behind the curve in bringing inflation down if it doesn't raise interest rates now.

"Inflation has been above target for more than five and a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward," Cook said in a speech in Santiago, Chile. "Waiting longer to implement rate increases risks getting behind the curve."

Cook dissented in October for the first time against the Fed's decision to hold rates steady.

On Friday, she said that urgency, along with accommodative financial conditions, led her to dissent last month. Cook said financial conditions are too accommodative at a time when inflation is stubbornly too high with no signs of coming down. She doesn't think rates are curtailing the artificial intelligence build-out, and she believes stock prices continue to support consumer spending. Holding rates steady again, Cook warned, would increase inflation pressure.

Cook pointed to inflation reports since the Fed's last policy meeting on Oct. 28, which show prices are rising briskly in a broad range of categories — including airfare, appliances, furniture, hotels, and restaurants. She estimates that the Fed's favored inflation measure — the Personal Consumption Expenditures index — rose 3.8% in October. Stripping out volatile food and energy prices, she estimates PCE rose an estimated 3.2% on a "core" basis.

Cook said the core measure shows that, while energy prices have risen due to the conflict in the Middle East, the sources of price pressure are varied.

She stopped short of providing any specific outlook on what the Fed should do at its meeting in December. Fed Governor Chris Waller has raised the prospect of raising by a jumbo 50 basis point hike .

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC Friday that the Fed should be forward-looking, given that energy prices are dropping.

articles.title: People urged to share views on Guernsey's online safety policy
articles.summary: The States wants to know if islanders want to be included in the social media ban for under-16s.
articles.body:
Islanders are being encouraged to share their views about the future of Guernsey's online safety policy.

The UK Government announced plans to add provisions to the online safety act that would ban social media platforms for under-16s from March 2027.

The Bailiwick of Guernsey is not included in the plans but the Policy and Resources Committee is exploring whether the act, or parts of it, might be extended to the island.

Deputy Lindsay de Sausmarez, P&R President, said the islands' position needed to be sought promptly on whether islanders would want to be included, particularly the thoughts of young people who would be directly affected.

In the UK apps including TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram are due to become inaccessible for under-16s in the spring .

The States has published a survey to help establish the island's position on the proposal - it is due to run until 21 December.

The proposal must be taken to the States in early 2027 if the bailiwick's position is to be made clear in advance of the UK implementing changes in March.

The government said while the short timeframe for establishing a position means it is not possible to undertake more extensive engagement with young people before the end of the year, the survey will be promoted as widely as possible to encourage young people - aged 13 and up - to take part.

De Sausmarez said if the Bailiwick decided it wanted to be included there could be no guarantee that social media providers would apply the restrictions.

"Equally the reverse position is also possible: providers may not necessarily distinguish bailiwick users from UK users when introducing changes in response to the legislation."

She said it was "important" the States conveys the bailiwick's position on "whether we'd want to be included or not, and if so, to what extent - as soon as possible to inform the UK government's discussions with online providers".

articles.title: Meta reevaluating its net zero goal amid AI boom
articles.summary: Meta is reconsidering its goal of hitting a 2030 deadline for net zero emissions, citing an increase in demand for AI infrastructure growth in the company’s annual sustainability report. “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets —…
articles.body:
Meta is reconsidering its goal of hitting a 2030 deadline for net zero emissions , citing an increase in demand for AI infrastructure growth in the company’s annual sustainability report .

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets — so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” the company said in the report signed by Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability.

“The path forward is complex, and the route may continue to evolve, but the outcomes we are working toward remain unchanged: to establish a long-term pathway to net zero emissions, to restore more water than we consume, and to build infrastructure in a way that supports surrounding communities and grids,” the statement continued.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The company noted that the net zero emissions goals were set with the anticipation of steady growth, falling clean energy costs and other changes in the broader system, but “the reality has been far more complex.”

“Demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected,” the report said, adding that meeting the demands meant “building at a pace and scale the industry has never attempted.”

In 2025, the company’s net emissions were 11.8 million metric tons, which “represented a year-over-year increase of 45%,” according to the report.

Last month, a United Nations climate report projected that global temperatures are set to exceed 1.5-degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels and this can be limited to “lowest possible” overshoot, but it would require urgent and steep cuts to emissions.

To limit the overshoot, global greenhouse gas emissions would have to be reduced by 18 percent by 2030, 45 percent by 2035 and 69 percent by 2040, relative to 2025 levels, according to a press release from the United Nations Environment Program.

“By contrast, the full implementation of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) would only reduce emissions by 5-8 per cent by 2030 and 11-15 per cent by 2035, relative to 2025 levels,” the release said.

If countries follow their current policies, warming levels could reach 2.8 degrees Celsius within the century and increase after, according to the U.N. report.

A recent study conducted by researchers from Harvard shows that the top 400 U.S. data centers emitted more greenhouse gases last year than Denmark.

articles.title: Ford reopens Canada auto plant, defying Trump tariffs
articles.summary: Ford on Friday reopened a Canadian auto plant following a $3.5 billion retooling project, defying President Donald Trump's efforts to force auto companies to...
articles.body:
Ford on Friday reopened a Canadian auto plant following a $3.5 billion retooling project, defying President Donald Trump's efforts to force auto companies to make vehicles stateside.

The plant in Oakville, Ontario, west of Toronto, was upgraded during a two-year production shutdown to make "Super Duty" pickup trucks, a massive boost for a Canadian auto sector starting to buckle under the weight of Trump's tariffs.

"We believe in Canadian manufacturing," Ford Canada CEO Bev Goodman told the crowd at the opening ceremony, stressing "the value of an integrated North American manufacturing network."

Goodman said the iconic American auto company has operated in Canada for 122 years -- nearly all of its existence.

Since returning to office last year, Trump has imposed stiff tariffs on parts and vehicles made in Canada while demanding that auto companies return production to the United States.

Those punitive measures have been a major sticking point in US-Canada trade negotiations, which broke off in August but have gathered renewed momentum in recent weeks.

Canada's federal and provincial governments have committed a combined CAD$464 million (US$324 million) to the Oakville plant's retooling project.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, a headline-grabbing Trump antagonist throughout the trade war, said the plant's reopening "shows we are fighting back and we are standing up for Canada."

Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly said Ford's commitment to Oakville shows "Canada is an auto nation" and intends to remain one.

Joly was due to meet later Friday with the chief executive of auto giant Stellantis, which is scaling back production in Canada in response to Trump's tariffs.

Stellantis -- which owns Chrysler, Jeep and Fiat -- abandoned plans last year to make the Jeep Compass in Brampton, Ontario, moving production of the model to Illinois.

It confirmed on November 9 that it was selling the Brampton auto assembly plant to a defense company, shuttering a facility that had employed nearly 3,000 people.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called Stellantis's actions a "betrayal." It is unclear whether Ottawa has a path to block the sale.

articles.title: Consistent bedtimes could protect your heart health, new study
articles.summary: Surprisingly, sleep duration was not associated with any major heart-related risks.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The consistency of your sleep schedule may be more important than the number of hours slept in preventing adverse heart events, according to a new study.

The research, published in Circulation: Population Health and Outcomes, looked at over 10,000 participants who wore a Fitbit over the course of six months. Researchers broke down sleep data by quality, quantity, regularity, timing and number of sleep cycles.

Night-to-night changes in sleep timing were linked to a 20-23 percent increased risk of a serious heart event. These risks included heart failure , acute myocardial infarction, cardiomyopathy and ischemic strokes.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Each 29-minute increase in sleep length from night to night increased the likelihood of a serious heart event by 24 percent. Specifically, researchers observed a 20 percent increased risk of heart failure and a 29 percent increased risk of cardiomyopathy.

Surprisingly, sleep duration was not associated with any major heart-related risks.

These findings challenge the age-old notion that the most important factor in healthy sleep is how many hours you get.

“Our finding is surprising because we can see the dominance of regularity instead of quantity,” lead researcher Nguyen Minh Tuan Viet, MD, PhD said in a press release. “Adequate quantity of sleep had some protective effect, but lack of sleep did not have much harmful effect in the study.”

The study did not establish cause and effect, but they point out a key controllable aspect of sleep that people can use to protect their health. However, more research is needed to establish if intervention lowers the risk of heart-related issues.

“Sometimes we can’t control the total amount of sleep, but the regularity- that is the thing that we can actively control,” Nguyen said. “But the regularity- consistent bedtimes throughout the week and waking up at the same time every morning, is something some people can control.”

articles.title: New report highlights mental health struggles of NHL goalies
articles.summary: Former NHL goalie Corey Hirsch told NewsNation mental health is a very real concern among players.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A new report highlighting the mental health struggles faced by goalies in the National Hockey League (NHL) found nearly a third of all players publicly known to have sought support from the NHL Players’ Association assistance program were goalies.

Former NHL goalie Corey Hirsch told NewsNation it’s a very real concern among players and that mental illness doesn’t discriminate.

“The thing about mental health is it doesn’t discriminate. It doesn’t care if you’re a broadcaster, a doctor, a lawyer. It doesn’t care if you have a hundred million dollars in your bank account or if you have $5 in your bank account,” he said.

Hirsch, a former goalie with the New York Rangers, Vancouver Canucks, Washington Capitals and Dallas Stars, added that he too has struggled with mental health issues in the past.

“But the problem is reaching out for help, right?” he continued. “That’s the mentality; it’s so cutthroat in professional sports that there’s a guy waiting right behind you to take your job. So that’s probably the main issue is reaching out for help, but it seems to be more prevalent with goaltending.”

The Athletic’s report highlights goalies are frequently the brunt of online harassment, including death threats to themselves and their families.

“The goalie is the last line of defense. So, they’re going to blame them … but the death threats and stuff? I mean, that has to stop,” Hirsch told NewsNation.

He added, “Why would you even do that? Like, why would a person do that to another human being?”

articles.title: Watchdog says AI smart glasses may violate your privacy
articles.summary: A Dutch privacy watchdog is warning consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A Dutch privacy watchdog is warning consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after an investigation found security vulnerabilities, privacy concerns and potentially dangerous advice from the devices.

The Netherlands’ Data Protection Authority examined six models available in the country and advised consumers Thursday not to buy the technology, citing risks to both users and bystanders.

The regulator found that some smart glasses could record people without their knowledge or consent.

Several models also had security vulnerabilities that could allow someone nearby to connect to the devices without permission, access recordings or even control the cameras.

The investigation raised concerns about the reliability of AI-generated advice.

In one simulated medical emergency, a pair of smart glasses told a user an ambulance was on its way, even though none had been called. Another pair offered inappropriate advice about an adult dating a minor.

The study warned that inaccurate information could have serious consequences when users rely on the technology in emergencies.

Are AI smart glasses facing more scrutiny?

The findings come amid growing concerns about the privacy implications of wearable technology.

In October, Dutch consumer rights groups filed a lawsuit against Meta, alleging its smart glasses violate privacy laws. A preliminary hearing is scheduled for Nov. 26.

Meta has previously said its camera-equipped glasses feature a blinking light that cannot be turned off while photos or videos are being captured.

In October, Dutch eyewear retailer Hans Anders also suspended sales of Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses in the Netherlands and Belgium over privacy concerns.

The Dutch regulator did not identify the manufacturers of the six models tested.

While the agency can fine companies for violating data protection laws, it does not have the authority to independently impose a total ban on smart glasses .

articles.title: Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Techies are building technology that can advance all aspects of the world — but can they protect their hearts? That's the vulnerability that honey pots exploit.
articles.body:
Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk.

“Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.

That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.

But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”

Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.

After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.

And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said.

Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”

What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.

“Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.

Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.

Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.

“AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”

The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said.

“Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.”

Carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information.

Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?”

It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the company.

Brown added that company culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter said.

“Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown said. “Paranoia doesn’t help. Recognizing you’re a target does.”

articles.title: Exclusive-Lutnick asked battery startup Pure Lithium to accept US takeover, documents and source say
articles.summary: Nov 20 (Reuters) - US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asked battery startup Pure Lithium in July to give Washington a 51% controlling stake in exchange for...
articles.body:
Nov 20 (Reuters) - US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asked battery startup Pure Lithium in July to give Washington a 51% controlling stake in exchange for funds to build a manufacturing plant that the company would not own or control, according to documents reviewed by Reuters and a person with direct knowledge of the request.

The company rejected the proposal, saying such a stake would likely garner public scrutiny, risk future capital-raising and outweigh any benefit ‌to shareholders, the documents from July and August showed.

"51% is far outside precedent and invites scrutiny," Pure Lithium's legal counsel Skadden Arps wrote in an August 22 memorandum reviewed by Reuters that outlined Lutnick's request.

The federal government's unsuccessful attempt to take majority control ‌of Pure Lithium has not been previously reported.

Lutnick's plan marks one of the latest moves by the ​Trump administration to acquire a stake in an American company and comes as the secretary and former investment banker faces increased scrutiny over his ties to corporate executives and companies affected by decisions made by his department.

The Trump administration has taken stakes in several companies since Donald Trump returned to the White House, including chipmaker Intel, extending its reach into the private sector in a way recent administrations have not.

However, it has not taken a majority stake in any company, with its most serious effort a proposed rescue of Spirit Airlines, the low-budget airline that ceased operations in May. Thus far, the largest equity stake the Trump administration has agreed to would give it a 15% stake in rare earths company MP Materials, which would make it the largest shareholder.

A Pure Lithium representative, when asked about the proposal, did not dispute the account.

The Commerce Department did not respond to ‌questions about the proposal posed by Reuters for this story.

It is not illegal for the federal ⁠government to acquire equity stakes in a private company and the administration has defended these efforts, particularly through using funds stemming from 2022's CHIPS Act, which was designed to boost domestic research and manufacturing of semiconductors.

Lawmakers opposed to the practice, though, contend the law never authorized such ownership. No court has ruled on the question.

articles.title: Court formally approves $7.25B class settlement for cancer claims from Roundup weed killer
articles.summary: A judge Friday formally approved a proposed $7.25 billion agreement to settle current and future cancer claims related to exposure of Monsanto’s Roundup weed killer. The decision, by Missouri Judge Timothy Boyer, wraps up years of litigation in which people alleged that their exposure to Roundup caused them to develop blood cancers known as non-Hodgkin…
articles.body:
A judge Friday formally approved a proposed $7.25 billion agreement to settle current and future cancer claims related to exposure of Monsanto’s Roundup weed killer.

The decision, by Missouri Judge Timothy Boyer, wraps up years of litigation in which people alleged that their exposure to Roundup caused them to develop blood cancers known as non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

The judge described the settlement as being “among the largest in history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements.”

Monsanto and the plaintiffs suing it reached the settlement agreement in February and received preliminary approval in March.

After the agreement and preliminary approval, the Supreme Court made it more difficult for some similar cases to be heard in the future. It particularly ruled that people cannot sue pesticide companies for failing to warn of health impacts not formally recognized by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

The EPA has not linked glyphosate, a key ingredient in Roundup, to health impacts like cancer. In 2015, the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer described it as “probably carcinogenic” to humans.

Boyer cited the Supreme Court’s decision in his final approval of the settlement agreement, saying that even without it, Monsanto has won a majority of related cases.

Christopher A. Seeger, a court-appointed lawyer for one of the subclasses in the case, praised the decision as helping people who were exposed to the weed killer.

“Today’s final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice,” Seeger wrote in a statement.

Meanwhile, Bill Anderson, the CEO of Bayer, which owns Monsanto, described the approval as “a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation,” in a written statement.

Pesticide issues, including those related to glyphosate, have also become a major cause of the Make America Healthy Again movement linked to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The Trump administration backed Monsanto at the Supreme Court.

articles.title: Virginia reports first measles-related death of 2026
articles.summary: A young child in Virginia died after testing positive for measles, the state’s health department said Friday, marking the first death tied to the illness in the state this year. The department said the child was aged 0-4 but declined to share further identifying information, such as vaccination status or other details related to the…
articles.body:
A young child in Virginia died after testing positive for measles, the state’s health department said Friday, marking the first death tied to the illness in the state this year.

The department said the child was aged 0-4 but declined to share further identifying information, such as vaccination status or other details related to the death, due to privacy concerns.

The fatal case in Virginia is the second reported measles-associated death since the Pan-American Health Organization announced this week it revoked the U.S.’s measles elimination status, declaring the disease endemic amid an ongoing outbreak.

In 2026, states have reported a total of 12 deaths tied to the disease, though the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) currently count currently sits at six as of Friday night.

The discrepancies between these reported death tolls have become a source of contention between state officials and federal ones, specifically Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — who has sent mixed signals on the administration’s vaccine stance in recent months.

Virginia has recorded 220 measles cases so far this year, with just 1 percent in unvaccinated individuals, according to the commonwealth’s dashboard . More cases are concentrated in Charlotte County, a rural county in Southside Virginia, than anywhere else in the state.

Only a few patients have been hospitalized statewide, and the University of Virginia medical center revealed Monday it was treating a patient with measles — warning students to isolate if they develop symptoms and check their vaccination status.

But no state has been hit harder with the measles outbreak than Pennsylvania, which accounts for more than 25 percent of cases in the entire country and a majority of states’ reported deaths.

The CDC continues to say the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the most effective way to fight the infection, but just a few months ago, Trump signed an executive order recommending breaking up the MMR vaccine into three doses. The shot is typically given once at 12-15 months and again at 4-6 years.

At an event in the Oval Office in August, Trump suggested the combined shot was “lethal” without providing any evidence.

articles.title: TJMaxx’s parent company is spending one-third of its $463 million in tariff refunds on corporate bonuses—and it’s not the only one
articles.summary: In total, $167 million of TJX’s total refunds will be spent on compensation and bonuses, according to its financial disclosures.
articles.body:
TJX , the parent of TJ Maxx and Marshalls, has now set aside $167 million of its $463 million in tariff refunds for bonuses and incentive pay, the company disclosed Wednesday —and it plans to keep booking bonus costs next quarter, even though it isn't expecting any more refunds. The discretionary bonuses are for "non-executive" associates, according to the filing.

The move follows what U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told companies to do back in March : pass refunds along to workers as a bonus or a raise, "because that's the purpose of the program," he said.

Giving tariff refunds back to employees raises questions about whether consumers will see refunds reach their wallets. A Federal Reserve Bank of New York analysis found nearly 90% of the tariffs' economic burden fell on U.S. firms and consumers. TJX hasn't said it will lower prices.

TJX isn't alone. As U.S. companies scrape back more than $100 billion in tariff refunds, some are using those rebates for company bonuses rather than passing them back down to customers who bore the brunt of the levies.

Publicly traded companies, including Titleist-maker Acushnet, and industrial tool producer Stanley Black & Decker, have disclosed plans to use millions of dollars returned to dole out to employees, including executives. ProPublica, which first reported the trend this week, identified at least nine public companies doing the same.

While some companies , such as FedEx , have pledged to give the cash from the refunds back to consumers, and companies like Walmart and Target have committed to lowering prices as a result of receiving refunds, others are spending chunks of the money internally.

Which companies are using tariff refunds for bonuses?

TJX, which recovered $463 million in aggregate tariff refunds, reported accruing $112 million in incremental expenses in the second quarter of fiscal 2027 for "year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible Associates globally," and an additional $55 million for compensation and bonuses in the third quarter , which it reported earlier this month. In total, $167 million, about one-third of its total refunds, will be spent on compensation and bonuses.

The company said it would use the remaining $296 million in refunds "to support our future growth," but did not say it would lower prices or pass down rebates to consumers.

"As part of our off-price retail model, we offer consumers prices that are generally 20%-60% below full-price retailers' (including department, specialty, and major online retailers) regular prices on comparable merchandise," a TJX spokesperson told Fortune in a statement.
