articles.title: President Donald Trump's Economy and the AI-Driven Stock Market Are in Trouble, Thanks to a Newly Identified Source of Inflation
articles.summary: Elevated inflation is no longer just a Trumpflation story.
articles.body:
The stock market has endured some of its most volatile days in history under President Donald Trump. Nevertheless, the iconic Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI), benchmark S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), and tech-fueled Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) have averaged higher returns under Trump than under most other presidents since the late 1890s.

Some of this outperformance can be traced directly to Trump's policies. The signing of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act into law in December 2017 slashed the peak marginal corporate income tax rate from 35% to 21%, leading to record share buybacks by S&P 500 companies.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But the bulk of Wall Street's gains comes courtesy of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution and the ongoing AI data center build-out. AI is the largest addressable opportunity investors have ever seen, which explains why the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite have blasted to several record highs.

Persistently elevated inflation is a serious problem for President Trump's economy and Wall Street. Image source: Official White House Photo by Andrea Hanks, courtesy of the National Archives.

Both President Trump's economy and the AI-driven stock market are in trouble, with persistently elevated inflation to blame. If Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) get aggressive with interest rate hikes, it would likely spell the end of a four-year (and counting) bull market.

The issue is that elevated inflation is no longer just a Trumpflation story. The central bank has identified a new source of inflation that's put FOMC policymakers in quite the pickle.

Trumpflation is becoming entrenched in the broader economy

Keep in mind that when the U.S. economy is growing, a modest level of inflation is expected. It's a positive thing when strong demand for goods and services gives businesses some degree of pricing power.

But the theme of 2026 has been one of persistently elevated inflation. Whereas the FOMC aims for a "timely return" to the 2% long-term inflation target, Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE), the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, reached a three-year high of 4.1% in May and has been moving in the wrong direction, yet again, in recent months.

articles.title: Democrats want ‘Medicare for More.’ Then comes the hard part
articles.summary: Democrats are coalescing around a plan to expand Medicare coverage to more Americans when they take control of Congress in January, a consensus policy that could bridge a divide between the party’s liberal and moderate wings. Both sides agree that they want to pursue “Medicare for More” quickly next year. But as Democrats eye ways…
articles.body:
Democrats are coalescing around a plan to expand Medicare coverage to more Americans when they take control of Congress in January, a consensus policy that could bridge a divide between the party’s liberal and moderate wings.

Both sides agree that they want to pursue “Medicare for More” quickly next year. But as Democrats eye ways to quickly lower costs, internal divisions over whether to push for “Medicare for All” could complicate a longer-term agenda for healthcare reform.

Last week, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), whom Democrats nominated to be Speaker next term, outlined a plan to lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, cover children under 18 years old and expand Medicare coverage for dental, vision and hearing benefits.

Jeffries also emphasized an immediate focus on reversing Medicaid cuts under the GOP’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and restoring the Affordable Care Act’s (ACA) temporary enhanced premium tax credits that expired at the end of last year .

“Right out of the gate, we will aggressively work on fixing the extraordinary damage that’s been done,” Jeffries said during a press conference Tuesday. “But we also know, as Democrats, that a return to the status quo is not acceptable.”

In the past, Democrats have been split between those who support Medicare for All and those who prefer incremental changes that don’t eliminate private insurance.

Buoyed by the victory of candidates like Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) in Michigan, progressives in the House and Senate are expected to make a significant push for single-payer healthcare.

But at least for now, the factions appear united in moving toward a more middle ground.

Lawmakers in the Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC) welcomed what Jeffries outlined but emphasized they believe it’s only the first step in the broader march toward single-payer healthcare.

Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.), a CPC member, said he believes Jeffries’s immediate Medicare expansion plan is “very achievable.”

“I think we have such a large majority that this step forward is going to be something that we’re going to be able to accomplish,” he said. “But our first step is undoing a lot of the Big Beautiful Bill stuff.”

Frost noted that the incremental Medicare expansion proposal has also received support from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), the longtime standard-bearer for Medicare for All who is expected to chair the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions next Congress.

Sanders on Wednesday praised Jeffries’s Medicare expansion plan, dubbing it “the first year [of] Medicare for All.”

“I think the word is getting out that it is no longer, from a political point of view, from a policy point of view, good enough to tinker around the edges,” Sanders said. “Yes, we have to protect those people who lost their Medicaid, ACA premiums — I’m all in on that. But I think increasingly the American people and elected officials understand the current healthcare system is broken.”

Shortly after the elections, Sanders outlined his own plan to lower the Medicare eligibility age by 10 years, include vision and dental care in Medicare, and guarantee health insurance for all children through age 19.

El-Sayed also jumped in this week to back the House leader’s proposal as a “great start.”

The Michigan Democrat made instituting a single-payer healthcare system a key tenet of his Senate campaign.

While major change is unlikely in the next two years with President Trump still in office, advocates are looking to set the agenda with an eye toward the 2028 presidential election.

Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.), another CPC member, expressed uncertainty Thursday about the ability to get Trump’s signature on a Medicare expansion package.

“I don’t know if we’re going to be able to do very much with Trump, but I do think that the first steps are really critical, and putting back funding to an infrastructure that has been starved is important too,” Grijalva said.

The progressive lawmaker, who supports Medicare for All as a long-term goal, acknowledged the challenges associated with an immediate transition to a universal single-payer healthcare system.

“Ideally, we want to get to Medicare for All relatively quickly, but I even heard Sen. Sanders say if we just flip a switch, you know, we could collapse a system that is already struggling,” she said. “So we don’t want to do that.”

If the Medicare expansion idea gains traction in the next Congress, progressives will want to see real movement toward Medicare for All, something neither Jeffries nor Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) has endorsed. That would likely create internal tensions within the party as it looks ahead to the 2028 presidential election.

But at the same time, letting a bill come to the floor during the Trump presidency would catapult Medicare for All directly into the 2028 conversation and show Democrats no longer fear attacks about taking away people’s private insurance.

Rep. Ami Bera (D-Calif.), a physician and member of the centrist New Democrat Coalition, said a workable long-term plan will be contingent on factors like cost and coverage.

Bera stressed a more immediate focus on reversing cuts made under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, also known as H.R. 1.

“Those aren’t the long-term solutions, but those at least give us time to lower costs for Americans, increase access, and then I think we can work on the longer-term ideas,” he said.

As many adults and families struggle to afford health costs, the popularity of Medicare for All is growing. A KFF poll in September showed two-thirds of Americans favored a “single government plan.”

A national debate would likely include more details about costs and trade-offs that aren’t being captured in surface-level campaign slogans.

Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin (D) praised Jeffries’s plan as a “very meaningful and substantive proposal” that could bridge divides within the Democratic Party over long-term healthcare goals.

“It would undoubtedly win the support of a lot of people who want to move towards a national health system with Medicare for All, and I think it could gain a lot of support from other people who understand the huge gaps that exist,” Raskin said. “So I think that’s a shrewd proposal for him to advance.”

articles.summary: JPMorgan Chase says hackers accessed marketing data at third-party vendors as an extortion group leaks records tied to Visa and Mastercard customers.
articles.body: You trust your bank to protect your money. But how much do you know about the outside companies that also handle your personal information? That's a question worth asking after a ransomware group leaked customer data linked to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase. On Nov. 19, 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported that hackers had leaked information allegedly linked to thousands of customers of the three financial companies. The reported exposure involved third-party service providers that work with the financial companies. Now, customers are left wondering what information hackers obtained and whether they need to take action. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. What happened in the Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan data leak? A cyber extortion group known as n0n claimed to have stolen information associated with the three financial companies. According to Reuters, the group posted claims on Nov. 16 about obtaining cardholder engagement records. These allegedly included extensive marketing activity associated with tens of thousands of email addresses. The group also posted claims involving Visa and Mastercard that same day. The reported cyberattack involved outside service providers that handle information for financial institutions. Some of the records appear connected to customer marketing activities and cardholder benefit programs. However, several important questions remain unanswered. The companies have not publicly identified all the affected vendors, and investigators have yet to establish whether one compromised provider was responsible for all three reported exposures. What JPMorgan Chase says about the cyberattack JPMorgan Chase confirmed that third-party service providers were targeted in a cyberattack. In a statement to CyberGuy, a JPMorgan Chase spokesperson said, "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses." The bank says its services remain operational. It also plans to contact affected customers where appropriate and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring. Addressing the transaction processing delays that affected multiple banks earlier this week, the spokesperson added, "There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week." According to Reuters, leaked records appeared to contain more than 16,000 JPMorgan Chase customer email addresses and 124 bank employee email addresses. Some entries also included phone numbers and postal codes. Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the records. Mastercard confirms limited customer information was exposed Mastercard also acknowledged an incident involving an outside provider. However, the company says the exposed information was limited to email addresses belonging to a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program. In a statement to CyberGuy, Mastercard said the incident involved non-payment information. "There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," Mastercard said. The company also confirmed that the exposure has been contained. Its teams are working with the affected provider to support cardholders as needed. Mastercard has not publicly identified the benefit program involved or disclosed an exact number of affected customers. The company also has not indicated that payment-card numbers were exposed. What Visa says about the reported customer data leak Visa has responded to CyberGuy about the reported cybersecurity incident involving a third-party service provider in the Asia-Pacific region. The company says its own systems and payment information were unaffected. In a statement, the company said, "Visa is aware of these claims. They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected. This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week." However, Visa has not identified the service provider or disclosed how many customers may have been affected. The company also has not specified what non-payment information, if any, was exposed. Could the data leak put your bank account at risk? So far, the companies' statements point primarily to customer information held by outside service providers. Mastercard says its payment network remains secure, while Visa says payment-card numbers were unaffected. JPMorgan Chase has identified potentially exposed marketing data. There has been no verified indication that customer banking passwords were stolen or that hackers accessed funds through this incident. However, stolen contact information can still create problems. Criminals may use names or email addresses to make phishing messages appear more convincing. You could receive an email claiming your bank detected suspicious activity related to the recent cyberattack. The message might direct you to a fake website designed to steal your login information. We've covered how convincing these scams can be in our article about fake bank security alerts that trick customers into sharing personal information. 9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE How to protect yourself after the Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan data leak You do not need to assume your account has been compromised. However, there are several practical steps I recommend taking to reduce your exposure to follow-up scams. 1. Watch for fake bank security alerts Be cautious of unexpected emails or text messages claiming your Visa, Mastercard or JPMorgan Chase account needs immediate attention. Scammers may reference a real cyberattack to make their messages more convincing. They could also claim that your card will be suspended unless you verify your information. Don't click links or open attachments in suspicious messages. Instead, open your bank's official app or type its website address directly into your browser. You can also call the number printed on the back of your card. Using strong antivirus software can provide additional protection by helping detect malicious links and downloads before they cause damage. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at CyberGuy.com 2. Never share a bank verification code A scammer may call pretending to be from your bank's fraud department. The caller might already know your name or email address and claim that a recent breach put your account at risk. The scammer may then ask you to read back a one-time verification code sent to your phone. That code could allow someone to access your account or approve an unauthorized transaction. Never share a verification code with someone who contacts you unexpectedly. Also, never transfer money to another account because a caller claims it will keep your funds safe. Legitimate bank representatives will not ask you to move your money to a supposedly safe account. 3. Turn on account alerts and review your transactions Enable transaction notifications through your bank or credit card app. These alerts can help you spot unfamiliar purchases without waiting for your monthly statement. Check your recent activity and report anything suspicious immediately. Even though the companies have not reported a compromise of their payment networks, monitoring your accounts remains a useful security habit. 4. Strengthen your passwords and account security Make sure your banking and primary email accounts use unique passwords. If you have reused passwords across accounts, replace them with strong alternatives. A password manager can help you generate and store them securely. Turn on multifactor authentication wherever available. If your bank supports passkeys or security keys, consider using them. An authenticator app is generally a stronger option than SMS codes, although it can still be vulnerable to certain phishing attacks. There is currently no verified evidence that passwords were exposed in this incident. These precautions can help protect your accounts against separate attacks. For more details, see our guide to whether bank text codes are enough to protect you. 5. Watch for official breach notifications JPMorgan Chase says it will contact affected customers where appropriate and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring. If you receive a breach notification, confirm that it came from your financial institution before clicking an enrollment link or sharing personal information. Credit monitoring can help you identify suspicious changes to your credit reports. However, it cannot stop someone from sending phishing emails or impersonating your bank. You should also be suspicious of anyone demanding payment to activate complimentary protection offered after a breach. 6. Consider a credit freeze if sensitive information was exposed A credit freeze makes it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts in your name. You can place one for free through Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. You must contact each credit bureau separately. A freeze does not affect your credit score, and you can temporarily lift it when you need to apply for credit. If only your name and email address were exposed, a freeze may not be necessary because of this incident alone. However, it can provide broader protection, especially if a breach involves more sensitive identifiers such as a Social Security number. 7. Reduce the personal information scammers can find about you An exposed email address becomes more useful to scammers when they can connect it with other personal details found online. Consider removing unnecessary information from public profiles and checking what data broker websites have collected about you. A personal data removal service can also help request the removal of information from participating people-search sites. These services cannot erase information already stolen in a cyberattack. However, reducing the amount of personal information publicly available may make it harder for criminals to build convincing profiles for targeted scams. You should also use your phone's spam filtering features and reputable antivirus software to help block suspicious messages or malicious downloads. articles.title: Swift assurances from officials after wave of nationwide outages raises questions, expert says
articles.summary: SMET CEO Danny Cooper says ruling out a cyberattack too fast risks missing hackers after the JPMorgan Chase, Microsoft outages and air travel ground stop.
articles.body: Amid a slew of high-profile disruptions that struck major pillars of American life over the past week, including a nationwide ground stop that halted air travel, banking outages at JPMorgan Chase and other lenders, and a service disruption at Microsoft, officials were quick to reassure the public that nothing nefarious was behind the failures. During the ground stop, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the homeland and the banking system remained secure, insisting that the disruptions showed no signs of a cyberattack or malicious activity. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton similarly stated that officials saw no evidence of a coordinated or state-sponsored attack, pointing instead to routine patching and system upgrades. DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE' "Based on what we know today … these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes," Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday. "They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack." Major companies, including Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase, also attributed the disruptions to internal technical issues or software bugs rather than malicious intrusions. US INFRASTRUCTURE CRUMBLES AS ADVERSARIES POWER UP – LEAVING AMERICANS DANGEROUSLY EXPOSED: CYBER EXPERT To Danny Cooper, CEO of critical infrastructure security firm SMET, the speed with which those assurances were issued poses a problem. "A blanket statement like 'there's no malicious activity associated with any of the outages' is almost impossible from a probability perspective," Cooper told Fox News Digital. THE OUTAGES AMERICA HAS SUFFERED WEREN'T AN ATTACK, BUT THE NEXT FAILURE COULD BE Public anxiety tends to spike around a single question in the aftermath of a major disruption: Was it a coincidence or an attack? Public skepticism is understandable given how many critical systems stumbled within a five-to-six-day window, Cooper said. "How plausible is it that all these pillars or whatever all suffered major independent technical failures within a five- or six-day window?" Cooper asked. "I think highly improbable. And I understand why the American public is calling this into question and deeply empathize with that. The pattern recognition is there." DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK Even when officials point to routine maintenance or aging hardware, Cooper argued that ruling out foul play too quickly skips investigative steps that take time to execute properly, which could potentially undermine efforts to fix vulnerabilities and prevent future incidents. "If a company or the government is making a statement that is as bold as 'we are certain there is no malicious activity here' without having the time to actually do an appropriate investigation, in the case of this sort of cyber domain, some cyber forensics and a full audit of what transpired, that's not quite how it works," she said. PERPETUAL PARALYSIS: WHY EVERYTHING IS GRINDING TO A HALT "On the physical side, being able to fully interrogate what has happened in the environment, who was there, and so on about what is happening in the periphery and what led up to that moment in time, those things take time." An instant "nothing to see here" message can also deepen public suspicion, Cooper said, particularly when multiple institutions and agencies echo that conclusion before audits can be completed. JOIN THE CHAT: RECENT TECH OUTAGES LOOM OVER MULLIN TESTIMONY ON WORLDWIDE THREATS The Democratic National Committee (DNC) also sounded the alarm over conflicting statements coming from the Trump administration. "The administration has repeatedly offered conflicting statements about the causes of the outages," DNC Deputy Communications Director Kendall Witmer said in a statement. "Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested that SI – Trump’s preferred name for Artificial Intelligence (AI) – is responsible for the multiple outages that have occurred in recent days, according to a "very smart" tech guy he talked to. Then, yesterday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio contradicted Mullin and would not attribute the outages to AI." MICROSOFT’S MASSIVE OUTAGE OFFERS A LESSON IN HOW TO BRING THE WORLD BACK ONLINE Much of the official explanation surrounding the November disruptions centered on software updates and system upgrades. Organizations frequently schedule maintenance and can experience downtime when rolling out changes at scale, especially if teams move too quickly, Cooper noted. However, those windows are what sophisticated adversaries watch closely, she warned. "If companies are disproportionately moving to execute these sorts of upgrades en masse, then yes, it's possible that you would have a higher number of downtime or outages," she said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "But it's also quite possible that, particularly given the sophistication of cyber adversaries, whether it's hackers, whether it's non-state entities, whether it's nation-state entities, it's also possible that they are using those software updates or upgrades or patches and in those moments actually injecting malware and exploits and so on."

articles.title: Former defense secretary suggests Iran war may last until 2029: ‘It’s just gonna take a long time’
articles.summary: Former Defense Secretary Mark Esper said on Friday the ongoing war in Iran would go into 2027 but questioned whether it could go into as far as 2029, noting it “takes time.” “Well, it’s definitely gonna go into 2027 … the question is, does it roll into 2028 and even 2029? Right, and it all…
articles.body:
Former Defense Secretary Mark Esper said on Friday the ongoing war in Iran would go into 2027 but questioned whether it could go into as far as 2029, noting it “takes time.”

“Well, it’s definitely gonna go into 2027 … the question is, does it roll into 2028 and even 2029? Right, and it all depends on the strategy,” Esper said during an appearance on NewsNation, the Hill’s broadcasting partner.

Esper said he has advocated for the strategy of an “economic blockade” that President Trump is pursuing, adding, “it takes a very patient disciplined strategy that’s internationalized and that you slowly choke out the Iranians so that they eventually come to the negotiating table in a credible way.”

He emphasized that the strategy seems to be working, citing high inflation in Iran and the considerable drop in Iran’s currency, Rial.

“It’s just gonna take a long time,” Esper said.

The conflict in Iran was a major issue for voters in the days leading up to the midterm elections, where Democrats secured a sweeping victory taking control of both chambers of the Congress. In a Gallup poll released before the midterms, roughly 77 percent of voters said the war would be an “extremely” or “very” important issue when casting their vote.

Following the GOP’s midterm losses, Vance placed the blame on the war saying, “The reason we lost is the war.”

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he added. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

On Friday, during a press conference following the president’s trip to China, Vance deflected on a question of whether the war was worth the GOP’s losses, saying, “The president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again.”

“The goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we should be doing. It’s the biggest state sponsor of terrorism,” Vance said, adding his “job is to support the president of the United States.”

Esper said Vance “clearly” does not support the war “fully the way the president would expect.”

He agreed with Vance’s initial assessment of the midterm results, saying, “It was very clear that the two top issues for the reason why Democrats came out and many Republicans either stayed home or voted for the other side was affordability and the Iran war.”

Esper warned that “losing both the house and Senate means that the Trump agenda is largely dead at least in domestic policy.”

“There’ll be constraints placed on him from a foreign policy perspective as the Democrats type appropriations,” he added.

articles.title: FBI looking into possible breach of its crime database: Report
articles.summary: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is looking into a potential breach of its nationwide criminal information database, a second breach in recent months coming on the heels of nationwide technology outages. The agency’s National Crime Information Center, which is used to connect federal, state and local authorities for nationwide information, was breached by apparent…
articles.body:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is looking into a potential breach of its nationwide criminal information database, a second breach in recent months coming on the heels of nationwide technology outages.

The agency’s National Crime Information Center, which is used to connect federal, state and local authorities for nationwide information, was breached by apparent hackers, according to a report from CNN on Friday .

The Hill has reached out to the FBI for comment.

The attack comes as the country is recovering from widespread technology outages in the past week which impacted flights, banks, internet services and more.

On Nov. 12, Microsoft faced global outages that impacted its platforms Outlook and Teams. A day later, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Authorities attributed FAA incident to an overload of data on routers.

Customers of several banks including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo had trouble accessing their accounts on Monday.

Speculations flared over whether the outages were linked to a cyberattack, but Trump administration officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, have repeatedly said that is not the case.

Even though officials have said cybercrime was not at the center of the recent outages, the phenomenon has certainly emerged in the recent months with multiple incidents related to hacking.

In September, the FBI was targeted by the group ShinyHunters, involving sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website, according to CNN . A cybersecurity executive and ransomware expert from Canada was arrested and is facing charges related to the attack.

Earlier this month, the FBI cracked down on North Korean hackers who had stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 ​months using a social engineering scheme called “FaceStealer.”

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance faced a $6.3 billion hack in October that prompted the company to suspend all deposits and withdrawals. It also led other cryptocurrency firms to freeze around $3 billion in assets .

Following the recent incidents, the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security announced a new hub to combat cybercrime on Wednesday.

“It gives investigators tools to triage victim complaints and map the networks responsible,” the Justice Department said in a statement.

articles.body:
Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick repeatedly ignored his warnings about U.S. AI chips being smuggled into China, long before reports surfaced about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“If Howard Lutnick wanted my support, perhaps he should have responded to my many letters warning about these Chinese communist front companies and, more importantly, taking the threats of communist China more seriously,” Cotton said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal published Friday.

Cotton, who recently won his reelection campaign in Arkansas and chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, told the Journal Lutnick and his deputies ignored correspondence for over a year about companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips, including Singapore-based company Megaspeed — at the center of Huang’s high-profile departure from the company.

The GOP senator said he sent a letter to Lutnick calling for an investigation into Megaspeed in October 2025.

Alice Huang, a former executive and major shareholder at Megaspeed, was accused of illegally smuggled AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with the former Nvidia CEO.

The tech giant’s chief resigned on Nov. 12 as these reports garnered national attention. The resignation came a day after The New York Times reported Huang had a separate affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.

The incident has sparked questions and calls for transparency on both sides of the aisle.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats, Reps. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (Calif.) and Gregory Meeks (N.Y.), are pressing Lutnick for information about the Commerce Department’s investigation into Megaspeed.

“The American public and Congress deserve a full accounting of what happened,” the lawmakers wrote in a letter to Lutnick Thursday.

On the Republican side, Rep. Brett Guthrie (Ky.), chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, requested earlier this week that interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress and Lutnick appear before the panel to answer questions.

articles.title: Alaska, your next governor is a Wikipedia nerd
articles.summary: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, Alaska's governor-elect, has made more than 13,000 WIkipedia edits.
articles.body:
We have arrived at a moment in American politics when people who are young enough to have grown up on the internet are being elected to office. That means there’s a lot more snooping into politicians’ online pasts to come. This month’s elections were no exception.

Earlier this month, 37-year-old Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the election for governor of Alaska , making him the first person to hold the office who was born in Alaska after it became a state in 1959. But when people went looking for more information about the Alaskan governor-elect, they didn’t find ill-advised tweets or compromising photos — they found out that he used to be an extremely active Wikipedia editor.

On a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011. The governor-elect is also from Alaska, went to Yale, and climbs mountains.

Wikipedia editors are an impressive community: They keep one of the most important sources of information online (mostly) clean and accurate. This only makes Kreiss-Tomkins look better as a legislator. Check this guy out! A dedicated public servant to the global constituency of Wikipedia! But a moderator on the Wikipedia subreddit pointed out that we cannot be 100% certain that this account is his.

“The odds that somebody would spend six years creating articles about Sitka, Alaska, Yale, and uploading PD photos of mountains, all to deceive people into thinking they were a disenchanted Howard Dean volunteer who was from Sitka, attended Yale, and was a mountaineer, is effectively zero. Plus they uploaded a photo of themself that looks like every other photo of JKT, minus the bald part,” one commenter replied.

Fair enough. If someone created a Wikipedia account pretending to be some guy in Alaska, made over 13,000 Wikipedia edits, and then waited two decades until that guy became the governor of America’s 49th state in order to sabotage him by making him look like a conscientious denizen of the web, kudos to them. But I’m a journalist. I have literal nightmares about getting stuff wrong. If you’re not careful, it’s easy to get duped.

So I emailed Kreiss-Tomkins, who is probably fielding many more important messages right now about policy, and asked if this is, in fact, his Wikipedia account.

So, there you have it, people of Alaska — your next governor is a nerd.

articles.title: Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10%
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fu...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates , hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.

"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."

Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers . The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.

Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House's affordability push . Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.

The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Trump's promise.

That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates.

In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money."

Other Democrats have endorsed the idea in various ways, including Rep. Maxine Waters of California, a powerful Democrat who sits on the House Financial Services Committee. Among Republicans, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri has proposed several caps on credit card interest rates, as recently as this year when Trump made his proposal.

"Congress should pass my bipartisan bill to cap these rates and deliver relief right away," Hawley said at the time.

Researchers who studied Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.

About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.

Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

articles.title: Trump says reported FBI database hack is ‘not good’
articles.summary: The FBI is reportedly investigating a hack of the National Crime Information Center.
articles.body:
The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), according to reports in CNN and the Associated Press .

The NCIC is the online database used by federal and local law enforcement to share information about warrants, background checks, and more. The scope of the breach does not yet appear to be clear.

A former FBI official told CNN that they’re not just concerned about “whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.”

President Donald Trump addressed the reports during an interview Saturday with Fox News, saying, “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good.” At the same time, Trump also said that as a result of the breach, “maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.”

In September, the FBI reportedly told agents and support staff that their personal information had been stolen in a cyberattack .

articles.title: The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’
articles.summary: Countries agree to ‘start discussing options’ for rules around autonomous weapons following UN negotiations in Geneva.
articles.body: One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations. According to NPR: > Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo. The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.” Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan. According to NPR, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions: > On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

articles.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Signal is limiting users' ability to take screenshots in both its Android and iOS apps.
articles.body:
Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.

Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”

“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”

Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

articles.title: Amazon is complaining about NYC Council on shipping labels, too
articles.summary: Amazon is taking its accusations that the New York Council is driving up prices offline and putting them on your packages.
articles.body: Amazon is leaving no venue unexplored in its fight against the New York City Council and the Delivery Protection Act. The company is now putting labels on shipments claiming that the Council could add up to $5 to any Amazon order. The Delivery Protection Act would effectively ban the sort of third-party arrangements Amazon currently uses to deliver many packages, including small companies and independent contractors. Last-mile delivery firms operating warehouses would need to be licensed by the city and directly employ their workers. Earlier this week, Amazon started showing notifications in its mobile app and on its website reading “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Now the company is including an almost identical message on shipping labels. Amazon claims that the bill, if passed, “would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City,” and has threatened to move its warehouses outside of the city. However, labor unions, Council Speaker Julie Menin, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have countered that the company is attempting to “threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council” and is acting out of “greed,” pointing to Amazon’s market cap of nearly $3 trillion.

articles.title: Rounds: Pentagon restricted socialization between US, Canada defense officials
articles.summary: The Department of Defense (DOD) recently issued a memo instructing its staff to limit social and informal interactions between U.S. and Canadian military personnel, Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said Saturday. During a press conference at the annual Halifax International Security Forum in Halifax, Nova Scotia, the South Dakota Republican said this order was drafted “several…
articles.body:
The Department of Defense (DOD) recently issued a memo instructing its staff to limit social and informal interactions between U.S. and Canadian military personnel, Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said Saturday.

During a press conference at the annual Halifax International Security Forum in Halifax, Nova Scotia, the South Dakota Republican said this order was drafted “several months ago” and “only recently signed.”

Rounds said the directive has no impact on formal military alliances, such as the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), NATO or The Five Eyes. Instead, it limits informal or social contact between American and Canadian officers.

“Really what this amounts to is, apparently, they were hoping that it would help promote and say, ‘Look, we really want you to bring up your defense spending,’” Rounds said.

The GOP lawmaker told reporters he and a delegation of four Democratic lawmakers at the summit met with Canadian partners, who expressed their ongoing effort to increase Canada’s defense spending.

“After listening to [the order], they said it sounds like it’s nothing new, nothing different than what they’ve been really practicing under for the last year-and-a-half,” he added.

Rounds said he didn’t believe the memo was intended for release and was more “a reaffirmation of what has already been, based upon our discussion with our Canadian friends.”

“Our goal up here is to find a way in which these types of memos are not necessary or issued in the future because of a renewed sense of cooperation between our two countries,” he added.

Democratic Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (N.Y.), Chris Coons (Del.), Tim Kaine (Va.) and Andy Kim (N.J.) made up the rest of the congressional delegation at the summit and spoke during the Saturday press conference.

Kaine, who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, called the tone of the memo “bad” and “unnecessary.”

“We understand this actually goes backaways and is just a formalization of something that is now months and months old,” he said. “I do think the new Congress is going to change the tone dramatically.”

Coons also expressed his hope that the next Congress could help bridge a path forward with Canada.

“I’m relieved this has no significant operational impact,” the Delaware lawmaker said. “But at the end of the day, as we’ve got our adversaries globally pulling together and working more closely — Iran, North Korea, China, Russia — the United States should be doing nothing to further aggravate some of the distance and division between the United States and Canada.”

articles.summary: Ahmedabad IT veterans quit amid AI job fears, launching ventures like namkeen, nankhatai, car perfumes and thrift stores to seek stability and returns.
articles.body: AHMEDABAD: Fourteen years into his IT career, Pratik Vaja got a warning he never expected. The US company where he worked as a senior developer gave employees three months to find new jobs, citing advances in artificial intelligence as the reason for the workforce reduction. Rather than searching for another software role, Vaja set off in a new direction and started selling namkeen. “Rising uncertainty around AI’s role in the sector prompted me to pursue entrepreneurship,” he said.Vaja spent a couple of months studying different businesses before launching his own namkeen brand. He now runs a store in South Bopal and also trades in around 200 varieties of namkeen. “A business requires more hard work, but it also gives higher returns,” he said. While Vaja’s decision followed a warning from his employer, other Ahmedabad techies are not waiting for AI to take their jobs. Many are leaving first, sensing that the industry where they built their careers may no longer offer the same security.Sweetu Kantariya, who spent more than a decade as a .NET developer, now runs a small nankhatai unit in Gota and has sold around 1,800 kg of the traditional biscuits since he started. Seeing how artificial intelligence was quickly changing software development, he knew it was time to create a future outside the industry that had defined his professional life.“About three months ago, I realised the impact of AI on my job and decided to start my own venture,” he said.His transition was not entirely sudden. While still employed, Kantariya would visit shops after office hours to explore potential orders, drawing on the experience of a cousin who runs a business in Rajkot. He eventually set up his own manufacturing unit, focusing on a single product.“IT has become a very difficult field because of AI. But the demand for good food will always be there. If we maintain quality, the business will grow. And above all, it is my own business,” he said.The exodus is not limited to developers. Designers and quality analysts across the city are also swapping their desks for businesses far removed from the digital world. For some, the decision has meant abandoning years of experience. For others, it has involved putting their savings at risk, with no guarantee that their new ventures will ever pay as well as their old jobs.Take Milan Soladhra, a software engineering graduate who joined the IT industry in 2013 and later worked as a quality analyst at an IT product company in the city. Six months ago, he chose to give AI the slip. He resigned and invested around Rs 20 lakh to launch a car perfume unit in Gota, near SG Highway.“The AI threat was growing. Before I could get a pink slip, I left my job and started my own business,” he said.The gamble is yet to pay off. “Right now, I earn less than I did in my job, but I believe this business has huge scope. Within a year, I will be able to earn as much as my job paid me,” he said. He is already planning to expand beyond car perfumes into other fragrance categories.For Divyesh Makwana, the decision to leave IT was driven as much by monthly financial obligations as by concerns about AI. After spending about nine and a half years in the industry, first as a designer and later as a team leader, Makwana decided he could not afford to wait. “I have EMIs to pay every month and cannot risk losing my earnings to AI, so I left my job in July,” he said.Makwana returned to Jamnagar, his hometown, where he opened a thrift store selling imported clothes after surveying local demand. Unlike several others, he has not completely severed his ties with the IT sector. articles.title: Kroger lays off American workers, moves jobs to India
articles.summary: The company is putting its relationship with its customers at risk as it tries to cut billions in expenses.
articles.body:
Kroger has started laying off about 3,000 American white-collar workers at the same time it's developing an operations center in India that is hiring dozens of workers.

That puts the company, which has described itself as "America's favorite grocer," at odds with how most Americans feel about U.S. jobs being outsourced overseas.

"Overall, when Americans are asked what hurts American workers, the top answers are outsourcing jobs to other countries (80% of Americans think this hurts U.S. jobholders), more foreign-made products being sold in the U.S. (77% think this hurts), increased use of contract or temporary employees (57%), automation of jobs (50%) and the decline in union membership (49%)," a 2016 Pew Research poll showed .

Kroger has already started notifying workers at its Cincinnati headquarters. It will also be making cuts in other cities where it maintains corporate offices, according to the Cincinnati Business Courier .

And while the cuts have already begun, the company has not shared a timetable for when the full 3,000 would be let go.

Kroger plans to cut about 3,000 corporate jobs over the next three years. In an internal memo, CEO Greg Foran wrote that the company has "more layers, more handoffs and more overhead than we need." He also said Kroger would use technology to improve efficiency and reduce duplicate work.

The company has, however, moved forward with its plans to launch an operations center in Bangalore, India, and has begun hiring workers there.

A request to Kroger Investor Relations to comment on this story was not immediately returned.

While sending jobs to India will help Kroger CEO Gregory Foran's plan to slash $5 billion in costs from the company that it plans to invest in lower prices, it's a move that risks alienating customers.

A research paper co-authored by Wharton marketing professor Stefano Puntoni "finds that consumers react far more negatively when layoffs are caused by offshoring. In other words, sending jobs abroad does not just affect the workers — it dents the company's image, too."

The paper's key point is based around what the researchers call the "social contract" — the unspoken expectation that firms should support the communities they operate in.

"When a company cuts domestic jobs and moves them overseas, consumers often view it as a betrayal of that norm — even if the move makes business sense on paper," Knowledge at Wharton shared .

That's something Puntoni talked about in an interview with Wharton Business Daily .

articles.title: Kenya’s internet metering bill raises privacy and affordability concerns
articles.summary: Kenya’s proposed internet metering law has prompted concerns over privacy, surveillance and rising connectivity costs.
articles.body:
Nairobi, Kenya – A proposed law requiring internet service providers in Kenya to monitor subscribers’ data consumption and introduce identifiable meter numbers has drawn opposition from industry and civil society groups, amid concerns about affordability, privacy and the handling of personal information.

The Kenya Information and Communications (Amendment) Bill, 2025, sponsored by Aldai MP Marianne Jebet Kitany, seeks to make consumption-based internet billing mandatory. It would require providers to assign each customer a unique meter number, monitor usage, convert it into readable details and issue invoices based on consumption.

The Bill’s stated objective is to protect consumers from unfair billing and ensure they pay for the internet they use. But the Communications Authority of Kenya (CA), telecommunications companies and civil society organisations have questioned whether mandatory metering is necessary and whether the proposed framework provides adequate safeguards for subscribers’ information.

The debate has intensified as the National Assembly’s Departmental Committee on Communication, Information and Innovation considers the legislation. The regulator has urged legislators not to make metered billing compulsory, while Telkom Kenya has warned of potential consequences for privacy, affordability and investment.

The Bill would require internet service providers to operate systems that monitor customer usage, convert consumption into readable details and generate invoices. Providers would also have to submit information about their billing systems, including subscriber meter numbers, to the regulator at least once every financial year.

The proposed provisions do not expressly require providers to record the content of private messages or the websites subscribers visit. However, civil society organisations have questioned what usage information would be collected and how identifiable records would be stored, accessed and shared.

The International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) Kenya has questioned the necessity of mandatory metering, arguing that the regulator already has powers to address billing complaints and protect consumers.

Demas Kiprono of ICJ Kenya has argued that the proposed system raises questions about whether the collection of identifiable usage information is necessary and proportionate to the Bill’s stated consumer-protection objective.

The concerns relate to the potential consequences of linking individual subscribers to records of their internet use. Critics say the legislation should specify who could access such information, how long it could be retained and the circumstances in which it could be disclosed.

Kenya’s Data Protection Act, 2019, already provides a framework for processing personal information. Opponents of the Bill say Parliament should make clear how those protections would apply to the proposed metering system.

Questions about telecommunications data have also featured in court proceedings involving university student David Ooga Mokaya.

He was arrested in November 2024 over a social media post concerning President William Ruto and charged with publishing false information. On February 19 this year, Senior Principal Magistrate Caroline Nyaguthii acquitted him under Section 215 of the Criminal Procedure Code, finding that the prosecution had not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

After his acquittal, Mokaya filed a petition at the High Court seeking protection of his personal information. He argued that information, including call data records, subscriber details, location data and metadata had been supplied to investigators without his consent. The allegations form part of the separate civil proceedings and should not be treated as a final judicial finding.

On February 25, Justice Bahati Mwamuye issued interim conservatory orders restraining the respondents and interested parties from transferring, sharing or disclosing Mokaya’s personal data without his written consent, a valid court order or an express provision of written law permitting disclosure.

The orders were issued pending further proceedings in the case. They do not establish that the proposed internet metering system would be used for surveillance. They do, however, illustrate the legal questions that can arise over the collection and disclosure of telecoms data.

Privacy is not the only concern. Mandatory consumption-based billing could also affect how households and businesses budget for connectivity.

In a submission to parliament on November 3, the Communications Authority cautioned against making metered billing compulsory across the sector. It said the approach could have unintended consequences for affordability, digital inclusion and consumer choice, particularly among low-income households, students, small businesses and communities in underserved areas.

The regulator noted that background applications, software updates, streaming and cloud services can consume data without users closely monitoring their usage.

Instead of prescribing one billing model, the Authority proposed usage alerts when subscribers reach 50, 80 and 100 percent of their data allowance, free real-time usage dashboards and monthly spending caps. It also recommended independent certification and periodic audits of metering systems, clearer itemised bills and stronger procedures for resolving billing disputes.

The Authority’s position is that consumer protection can be strengthened through regulations and licensing requirements without requiring every provider to adopt consumption-based pricing.

The financial impact of a change would depend on providers’ pricing and individual patterns of internet use. Customers who consume relatively little data could benefit from paying according to usage, while those who rely on large or continuous data allowances could face different costs. The Bill does not set the retail prices providers would charge.

Telecommunications companies have questioned whether the proposed changes could impose additional costs on providers and affect investment in broadband services.

Telkom Kenya Chief Executive Officer Mugo Kibati told the parliamentary committee on November 10 that mobile internet accounts for about 96 percent of data subscriptions and is already billed by volume. The proposed changes would therefore mainly affect fixed broadband services, which account for the remaining share, he said.

According to the Kenya News Agency’s report of the hearing, Telkom argued that a uniform metering framework could increase compliance costs and create risks for subscriber privacy and investment.

The company proposed that providers disclose their billing models, charges and fair-use policies before customers subscribe. It also called for free access to consumption information, itemised bills on request, effective dispute-resolution mechanisms and independent audits where billing accuracy is questioned.

Telkom further urged legislators to protect unlimited and speed-based internet packages, allow providers at least 18 months to comply with any new requirements and require aggregated rather than individually identifiable subscriber information to be submitted to the regulator.

Carole Kairuki, chief executive of the Kenya Private Sector Alliance, also raised concerns about the potential effect of mandatory metering on businesses. In an interview with Al Jazeera, she said changes to internet billing could increase compliance costs and make connectivity expenses less predictable for businesses, particularly smaller enterprises.

The Bill’s memorandum says the proposed amendments are intended to protect consumers from exploitation and secure their economic interests under Article 46 of the Constitution. It also states that the legislation does not limit fundamental rights and freedoms.

The disagreement is over whether mandatory metering is the most effective way to achieve that objective and whether the proposed provisions offer sufficient protection for subscribers’ information.

The debate comes amid wider public scrutiny of digital rights and the handling of online activity in Kenya, particularly following the 2024 protests against the Finance Bill. Kelvin Kubai, an Advocate of the High Court of Kenya, told Al Jazeera that internet access is important to young people’s civic participation and their ability to hold public officials accountable. He argued that any new regulatory framework should take those uses into account.

Parliament must weigh the Bill’s consumer-protection objective against concerns raised by the regulator, internet providers and civil society groups. The Communications Authority has proposed greater billing transparency, usage alerts and independent audits as alternatives to compulsory consumption-based billing.

Telkom CEO Kibati warned politicians against imposing obligations that could undermine a developing sector.

“Sometimes you can go overboard in trying to protect consumers that you actually kill a nascent, growing sector,” he told the parliamentary committee.

articles.title: Protesters storm Meta offices in India
articles.summary: Members of the youth wing of India’s Congress party stormed Meta offices and demanded that Meta reinstate its leaders’ Instagram accounts.
articles.body: Members of the opposition Congress party protested outside Meta’s offices in Delhi on Friday and appear to have entered the building in a video shared by CNN. Members of the party’s youth wing are demanding the company restore accounts of party leaders and warned of more protests to come. The Congress party has criticized Meta for censoring speech that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his BJP party disagree with, and has placed banners accusing Mark Zuckerberg of favoring BJP around the city. While two accounts in question were restored Friday, Manu Jain, who oversees social media for the party’s youth wing, told Reuters that “thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted.” [Media: In February, India issued tighter rules around the removal of “unlawful” content, changing the timeline from 36 hours to just three. Modi and the Indian government have long been criticized for their restrictive policies around free speech and accused of stifling opposition viewpoints and attempting to bully the press. Meta did not immediately return a request for comment.

articles.title: Trump hates wind power. A bill he supports may help it get built
articles.summary: While President Trump vows not to approve wind energy, a bill he could sign into law may have his administration moving these projects forward. articles.body:
While President Trump vows not to approve wind energy, a bill he could sign into law may have his administration moving these projects forward.

Trump has been a longtime opponent of wind energy, calling it “worthless.” However, he’s also encouraging Congress to approve the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which seeks to help energy sources of all kinds.

The legislation passed the Senate late Thursday night and now heads to the House, where it faces an uncertain future. If it passes the lower chamber, it will head to Trump’s desk.

Earlier this month, Trump told reporters that he “ 100 percent ” supports the bill. And on Friday, he touted it passing the Senate: “They had to get it through.”

However, asked earlier this month if he was OK with approving wind, which is among the energy sources the bill aims to bolster, Trump said, “No, I will not approve wind turbines.”

Yet, renewable energy backers are confident the Senate’s permitting reform bill will help wind farms gain and keep their approvals.

Thus far, the administration has repeatedly slowed down wind energy projects, including through roadblocks at the Department of Defense Department and the Interior Department.

Last year, the Pentagon stopped reviewing proposed wind projects, according to court documents. At the Interior Department, hurdles have included requiring every project to go through an extra layer of review at Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s office.

“Demand for electricity we assess to be growing at a rate that could surpass 50 percent over the next 15 years and also at the same time, most of that demand is being met, at least new capacity, from renewables,” said Frank Macchiarola, chief advocacy officer at the American Clean Power Association (ACP), during a recent event hosted by The Hill.

“But the pipeline is slowing down for those projects because the Trump administration has put a lot of roadblocks in the way of siting and permitting of renewable projects,” he said, adding that eliminating renewable energy tax credits in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act is also a factor in the slowdown.

Macchiarola’s organization and other proponents of renewable energy say that such slowdowns could be made more difficult in the future because of provisions in the legislation, if it passes.

They point to provisions that, for example, require federal agencies to decide whether or not to approve a project within 45 days of an environmental review and issue other authorizations within 120 days, making it so that federal agencies can’t hold up projects indefinitely by leaving them in limbo.

Gene Grace, ACP’s chief in-house legal officer, said that under BAAJA, agencies will be compelled to “move on timelines from one stage to another and importantly, there’s judicial enforcement if those timelines aren’t met.”

“I think that’s the real key because currently the way it works under the law, essentially agencies and administrations … have the discretion to deprioritize whatever technology and really for whatever reason they want,” Grace said.

Of course, at a decision point, the Trump administration could still deny a permit to wind projects, but Grace noted “it does require a certain level of evidence to be put in, so it can’t just be some type of arbitrary denial.”

He contrasted this to the Trump administration’s current policies toward wind.

“What we’ve seen over the last couple of years is a lot of denials that have been totally arbitrary or just freezing an industry using things like the secretarial review order or the DOD freeze to just kind of stop an industry without really any kind of reasoned explanation behind it,” Grace said.

He also pointed to a section of the bill that allows developers to sue the government if there’s a pattern of “disparate treatment” against a specific type of energy source and recoup certain costs.

The bill is also expected to prevent the Trump administration’s recent efforts to revoke existing permits from wind farms including offshore wind through a separate provision in the legislation.

At The Hill’s event, Xan Fishman, executive vice president of the energy program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said that the bill’s project certainty provisions mitigate risks for investors, who may be more willing to invest in wind or other types of energy projects.

“The whole point of it is to say, ‘If you get a permit, you can count on it’ … and of course on the front end, the process to get that permit can be in a reasonable amount of time,” Fishman said. “If you reduce those two degrees of uncertainty … the financing costs are lower, the construction costs are lower and so you get a lot more projects going forward.”

Questions have also been raised about whether the Trump administration will faithfully administer the bill or uphold an apparent side deal with Democrats to advance wind projects.

Rep. Scott Peters (Calif.), who is one of the Democrats who will be making the case in support of the bill to his House colleagues in the weeks ahead, said that wind supporters should feel more comfortable with the legislation than without it.

“Anyone who’s concerned about Trump jerking around wind and solar should be more comfortable with BAAJA and Trump than without” the legislation, he said.

“I know he’s not always someone who obeys the rules,” Peters added. “What I’d say there is that … Trump is a two-year problem. We’re trying to solve a 30-year problem, a 40-year problem with transmission and the build out of our energy infrastructure.”

Nat Keohane, president of Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, similarly said that people should focus on the administration’s actions.

“I know the president has said things, even in recent weeks, but what we’ve seen is the administration has been releasing projects,” he said.

“I think everybody understands that the focus of this bill and the purpose of this bill is to get the politics out of permitting, and that means if you’re going to get the parts of that that the Republicans want … they need to follow through and hold up their end of the deal,” he said. “And then of course there are parts of the bill that are written to ensure that that is the case.”

The bill seeks to be technology neutral, helping renewable energy and fossil fuels projects alike get across the finish line. It also seeks to speed up development of energy and infrastructure projects by restricting lawsuits that would be filed on environmental grounds and loosening other environmental restrictions.

It’s the result of months of negotiation between bipartisan lawmakers, particularly receiving significant Republican support in part because of the boost to fossil fuel projects, which the Trump administration has championed.

The White House reiterated Trump’s support for the legislation this week.

“President Trump is delivering on his American energy dominance agenda by fixing America’s broken permitting system, ensuring affordable, reliable energy for generations of American families and businesses,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said. “The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will cut bureaucratic red tape, accelerate the delivery of infrastructure projects, lower energy costs for American families, and create high-paying American jobs.”

Keohane said that he has confidence in the bill’s provisions being followed through by the administration because he’s spoken to Democratic senators, such as Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), who said that their confidence in the bill comes from the Republican lawmakers being on board.

“I’ve heard Sen. Whitehouse talk about this both privately and publicly, that he feels part of what gives him confidence to move forward is that he has been backed and supported by senators of the Republican Conference,” Keohane said.

Whitehouse sponsored the bill, along with Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.).

“So if it’s good enough for him and he feels these assurances, then it’s good enough for us,” he said.

articles.title: US ports face onslaught of cyber attacks
articles.summary: A number of ports across the U.S. are reporting an onslaught of cyberattacks amid a growing number of AI-enabled attacks targeting notable infrastructure. The Port of Corpus Christi, Texas, which functions as the U.S.’s largest passage of oil exports, said it was targeted with “hundreds if not thousands” of attacks per day, according to reporting from…
articles.body:
A number of ports across the U.S. are reporting an onslaught of cyberattacks amid a growing number of AI-enabled attacks targeting notable infrastructure.

The Port of Corpus Christi, Texas, which functions as the U.S.’s largest passage of oil exports, said it was targeted with “hundreds if not thousands” of attacks per day, according to reporting from The Financial Times .

The port’s chief executive, Kent Britton, told the outlet that attacks surged from “known bad actor” countries and organizations that are searching for high-profile targets.

The attacks against Corpus Christi’s port went after its computer systems by attempting to find weaknesses. Attackers also sent phishing messages, posing as senior executives, to trick staff into allowing them access, per The Financial Times.

“They’re poking at our systems and trying to find vulnerabilities,” Britton said. “With AI, it’ll only get more complicated.”

He stated the port was seeking additional help from Washington but “if you’re playing defence, you have to get it right every time…if you’re planning offence, you only have to get it right once.”

The Port of Los Angeles – the country’s busiest port – similarly stated that in August it had stopped 120 million attempted attacks into its networks through network exploitation, credential harvesting and malware attacks, Bloomberg reported.

Executive Director Gene Seroka expressed that all potential attackers “have to do is to get it right one time” and that it was “front of mind every day.”

The port’s cybersecurity operations team has scaled up in recent years, now forming a seven-layer digital defense, he added, per Bloomberg.

This comes after the Department of Justice (DOJ) and Department of Homeland Security launched a hub to fight cyber criminals – connecting more than 30 federal agencies with hundreds of state and local partners.

“It gives investigators tools to triage victim complaints and map the networks responsible,” the DOJ said in a statement. “It also provides a direct channel to the private-sector organizations best positioned to facilitate outreach to victims and disrupt criminal operations, as well as dedicated technical support.”

The port of Corpus Christi didn’t respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.
